papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that ALBERT models internally encode numerical ordering in their embeddings, with evidence of logarithmic scaling, providing insights into model numeracy.
papers.key_findings:
ALBERT models use primary PCA axes to represent ordering of numbers, ordinals, and magnitude orders.
Representations are closer for higher values, indicating a logarithmic scale.
Numerals and textual counterparts form separate clusters but increase along the same direction in PCA space.
Orders of magnitude words are ordered correctly along the first PCA axis.
Ordinal terms are represented in correct order up to 'seventh', with decreasing separation for higher values.
papers.limitation: Focus on single-token numbers excludes decimals and larger numerical values.
future_direction: Quantify to what extent learned internal structures reflect interval and ratio scales.
Investigate contributions of model architecture and term frequency in the corpus.
Extend analysis to multi-token numbers and mathematical operators.
papers.abstract: It has been found that Transformer-based language models have the ability to perform basic quantitative reasoning. In this paper, we propose a method for studying how these models internally represent numerical data, and use our proposal to analyze the ALBERT family of language models. Specifically, we extract the learned embeddings these models use to represent tokens that correspond to numbers and ordinals, and subject these embeddings to Principal Component Analysis (PCA). PCA results reveal that ALBERT models of different sizes, trained and initialized separately, consistently learn to use the axes of greatest variation to represent the approximate ordering of various numerical concepts. Numerals and their textual counterparts are represented in separate clusters, but increase along the same direction in 2D space. Our findings illustrate that language models, trained purely to model text, can intuit basic mathematical concepts, opening avenues for NLP applications that intersect with quantitative reasoning.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: A Study of Cross-Lingual Ability and Language-specific Information in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What factors influence the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT, and does language-specific information exist in its representations?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies datasize and context window size as crucial factors for cross-lingual transferability in multilingual BERT, and introduces Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to manipulate language-specific information for unsupervised token translation and improved cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The cross-lingual ability of m-BERT is learned from longer dependency and requires a massive amount of data; language-specific information can be manipulated via simple shifts to improve cross-lingual transfer, opening a new direction for strengthening cross-lingual ability.
papers.key_findings:
With small pretraining data, BERT does not outperform non-contextualized embeddings in cross-lingual ability; with large data, BERT achieves superior cross-lingual alignment.
Breaking down long dependency (smaller window size) hurts cross-lingual ability when pretraining data is large, but helps when data is small.
Language-specific information exists in m-BERT representations and can be extracted via mean difference vectors.
Applying Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to hidden representations can control the output language of m-BERT, enabling unsupervised token translation.
Using MDS to shift representations improves cross-lingual transfer performance on XNLI for most languages, except those with high subword overlap with English.
papers.limitation:
MDS does not improve performance for languages with high subword overlap with English (e.g., Spanish, French) due to shared subwords having different meanings, indicating the need for a more delicate mechanism.
The quality of unsupervised translation using MDS is not acceptable; only token conversion rate is measured, not fluency or accuracy.
future_direction: Develop a more delicate mechanism for applying language-specific shifts that considers differences among vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Recently, multilingual BERT works remarkably well on cross-lingual transfer tasks, superior to static non-contextualized word embeddings. In this work, we provide an in-depth experimental study to supplement the existing literature of cross-lingual ability. We compare the cross-lingual ability of non-contextualized and contextualized representation model with the same data. We found that datasize and context window size are crucial factors to the transferability. We also observe the language-specific information in multilingual BERT. By manipulating the latent representations, we can control the output languages of multilingual BERT, and achieve unsupervised token translation. We further show that based on the observation, there is a computationally cheap but effective approach to improve the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT.

papers.title: The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning: Language Models Compare Numeric Properties in Linear Subspaces
papers.research_question: Do LLMs leverage the linear subspace of entity-numerical attributes when solving numerical reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs answer numerical reasoning questions by first extracting numerical attributes from a linear subspace in the activation space and then using these linear directions for comparison, as demonstrated via PLS regression and causal interventions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs utilize linearly encoded numerical attribute information in low-dimensional subspaces to answer numerical reasoning questions, as validated by causal interventions.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode numerical attributes (birth year, death year, latitude) in low-dimensional linear subspaces of the activation space.
These subspaces are used by the model when performing numerical reasoning tasks (comparisons).
Causal interventions in these subspaces can alter the model's comparison answers.
The findings hold across three different LLMs (Llama3-8B, Mistral 7B, Qwen2.5 7B).
The intervention effect is most pronounced in the early to middle layers of the models.
papers.limitation:
No thorough error analysis to understand the model's types of mistakes.
Experiments are restricted to three types of numerical attributes (birth year, death year, latitude).
Intervention success relies heavily on the choice of the scaling factor α, and its full sensitivity has not been explored.
future_direction: Conduct error analysis to understand model mistakes.
Investigate whether findings extend to a broader range of numerical properties.
Explore the sensitivity of the model's performance to the intervention hyperparameter α.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) utilize numerical attributes encoded in a low-dimensional subspace of the embedding space when answering questions involving numeric comparisons, e.g., Was Cristiano born before Messi? We first identified, using partial least squares regression, these subspaces, which effectively encode the numerical attributes associated with the entities in comparison prompts. Further, we demonstrate causality, by intervening in these subspaces to manipulate hidden states, thereby altering the LLM's comparison outcomes. Experiments conducted on three different LLMs showed that our results hold across different numerical attributes, indicating that LLMs utilize the linearly encoded information for numerical reasoning.

papers.title: Modular Arithmetic: Language Models Solve Math Digit by Digit
papers.research_question: What internal mechanisms do LLMs use to perform simple arithmetic tasks, specifically focusing on whether they employ digit-position-specific circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates digit-position-specific arithmetic circuits in LLMs, showing that LLMs solve arithmetic tasks digit by digit using modular circuits that causally control individual output digits.
papers.conclusion: LLMs perform simple arithmetic using modular, digit-position-specific circuits that operate independently, indicating a structured and compositional approach to arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs use distinct, digit-position-specific circuits for units, tens, and hundreds digits in addition and subtraction.
These circuits are causally involved, as targeted interventions selectively alter only the corresponding digit in the output.
The circuits exist across various model sizes and tokenization strategies, including both multi-digit and single-digit tokenization.
Addition and subtraction circuits rely on largely distinct sets of neurons.
Carry operations are handled separately from the digit-position circuits, suggesting additional mechanisms for carry propagation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to addition and subtraction, not addressing more complex operations like multiplication or division.
Focuses on MLP layers and does not account for the role of attention heads or other residual stream components.
Uses Fisher Score for neuron identification, which may not be the most precise method compared to gradient-based attribution.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex arithmetic operations such as multiplication and division.
Analyzing circuits responsible for composing digit-level results into final outputs.
Using more precise methods like gradient-based attribution for circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: While recent work has begun to uncover the internal strategies that Large Language Models (LLMs) employ for simple arithmetic tasks, a unified understanding of their underlying mechanisms is still lacking. We extend recent findings showing that LLMs represent numbers in a digit-wise manner and present evidence for the existence of digit-position-specific circuits that LLMs use to perform simple arithmetic tasks, i.e. modular subgroups of MLP neurons that operate independently on different digit positions (units, tens, hundreds). Notably, such circuits exist independently of model size and of tokenization strategy, i.e. both for models that encode longer numbers digit-by-digit and as one token. Using Feature Importance and Causal Interventions, we identify and validate the digit-position-specific circuits, revealing a compositional and interpretable structure underlying the solving of arithmetic problems in LLMs. Our interventions selectively alter the model's prediction at targeted digit positions, demonstrating the causal role of digit-position circuits in solving arithmetic tasks.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Are Structural Concepts Universal in Transformer Language Models? Towards Interpretable Cross-Lingual Generalization
papers.research_question: Can explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages enhance cross-lingual generalization in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) are implicitly alignable across languages in transformer LMs, and proposes a meta-learning method to explicitly align these concepts, improving zero-shot and few-shot cross-lingual generalization without updating the LM parameters.
papers.conclusion: Explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages via meta-learning improves cross-lingual generalization, achieving competitive performance and narrowing the gap between languages, particularly for low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
Structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) can be identified based on prototypes in a relatively low-dimensional space of LM representations.
These structural concepts are highly alignable across languages in both encoder-only (mBERT) and decoder-only (LLaMA) models, as measured by RSA and Procrustes analysis.
A meta-learning-based method to align conceptual spaces achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods on syntactic analysis tasks, especially benefiting low-resource languages.
The method reduces the performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages.
The approach provides insights into cross-lingual in-context learning and can be integrated with prompting to improve generalization.
papers.limitation: Variations in alignability between language pairs may stem from insufficient UD treebank data for approximating prototypes and degenerate representation spaces for certain languages due to inadequate pretraining data or tokenization deficiencies.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to other aspects of language to better accommodate linguistic diversity using self-supervised knowledge.
Exploring more expressive probing models to extract structural concepts, especially grammatical relations, from models like LLaMA.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited considerable cross-lingual generalization abilities, whereby they implicitly transfer knowledge across languages. However, the transfer is not equally successful for all languages, especially for low-resource ones, which poses an ongoing challenge. It is unclear whether we have reached the limits of implicit cross-lingual generalization and if explicit knowledge transfer is viable. In this paper, we investigate the potential for explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages to enhance cross-lingual generalization. Using the syntactic aspect of language as a testbed, our analyses of 43 languages reveal a high degree of alignability among the spaces of structural concepts within each language for both encoder-only and decoder-only LLMs. We then propose a meta-learning-based method to learn to align conceptual spaces of different languages, which facilitates zero-shot and few-shot generalization in concept classification and also offers insights into the cross-lingual in-context learning phenomenon. Experiments on syntactic analysis tasks show that our approach achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods and narrows the performance gap between languages, particularly benefiting those with limited resources.

papers.title: Why Can't Transformers Learn Multiplication? Reverse-Engineering Reveals Long-Range Dependency Pitfalls
papers.research_question: Why do transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication?
papers.core_contribution: By reverse-engineering a successful implicit chain-of-thought model, the paper uncovers that transformers fail at multiplication due to a lack of long-range dependencies, and demonstrates that an auxiliary loss providing the correct inductive bias can enable learning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers fail to learn multi-digit multiplication due to a pitfall in learning long-range dependencies with gradient descent and an auto-regressive loss, but this can be addressed with the correct inductive bias, as demonstrated by the auxiliary loss method.
papers.key_findings:
The ICoT model learns the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication, while standard fine-tuning does not.
The ICoT model encodes long-range dependencies via attention patterns that form a directed acyclic graph (attention tree) to cache and retrieve pairwise partial products.
The ICoT model implements partial products in attention heads as Minkowski sums and represents digits using a Fourier basis, forming an efficient pentagonal prism structure.
Standard fine-tuning converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies, causing loss to plateau on middle digits.
An auxiliary loss that supervises the prediction of a 'running partial sum' via a linear regression probe provides an inductive bias that enables the model to learn multiplication successfully.
papers.limitation: The suggested inductive bias is task-specific and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Developing generalizing inductive biases for tasks with long-range dependencies.
papers.abstract: Language models are increasingly capable, yet still fail at a seemingly simple task of multi-digit multiplication. In this work, we study why, by reverse-engineering a model that successfully learns multiplication via \emph{implicit chain-of-thought}, and report three findings: (1) Evidence of long-range structure: Logit attributions and linear probes indicate that the model encodes the necessary long-range dependencies for multi-digit multiplication. (2) Mechanism: the model encodes long-range dependencies using attention to construct a directed acyclic graph to ``cache'' and ``retrieve'' pairwise partial products. (3) Geometry: the model implements partial products in attention heads by forming Minkowski sums between pairs of digits, and digits are represented using a Fourier basis, both of which are intuitive and efficient representations that the standard fine-tuning model lacks. With these insights, we revisit the learning dynamics of standard fine-tuning and find that the model converges to a local optimum that lacks the required long-range dependencies. We further validate this understanding by introducing an auxiliary loss that predicts the ``running sum'' via a linear regression probe, which provides an inductive bias that enables the model to successfully learn multi-digit multiplication. In summary, by reverse-engineering the mechanisms of an implicit chain-of-thought model we uncover a pitfall for learning long-range dependencies in Transformers and provide an example of how the correct inductive bias can address this issue.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Capture Language-Specific Concepts Across Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: What language-specific features exist in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, and how can they be identified and analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-LAPE, a method to identify language-specific features in the feed-forward networks of multilingual LLMs, showing these features are interpretable, influence model behavior, and can be used for language identification.
papers.conclusion: SAE-LAPE can identify interpretable, language-specific features in multilingual LLMs that causally influence model behavior and can be applied to tasks like language identification.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific features exist and are interpretable, primarily located in middle to final layers of the model.
Suppressing language-specific features increases perplexity in the corresponding language, while activating them can shift the model's output towards that language.
Language-specific features can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText, while offering more interpretability.
Features show a hierarchical processing of linguistic information, from morphemes in early layers to complex sentence structures and discourse patterns in deeper layers.
Some features capture stylistic patterns (e.g., conversational vs. formal) and language-specific cultural or geopolitical concepts.
papers.limitation: Interpretations of features may be biased toward the top activating examples, which could come from languages other than the primary one the feature is associated with.
papers.abstract: Understanding the multilingual mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) provides insight into how they process different languages, yet this remains challenging. Existing studies often focus on individual neurons, but their polysemantic nature makes it difficult to isolate language-specific units from cross-lingual representations. To address this, we explore sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for their ability to learn monosemantic features that represent concrete and abstract concepts across languages in LLMs. While some of these features are language-independent, the presence of language-specific features remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce SAE-LAPE, a method based on feature activation probability, to identify language-specific features within the feed-forward network. We find that many such features predominantly appear in the middle to final layers of the model and are interpretable. These features influence the model's multilingual performance and language output and can be used for language identification with performance comparable to fastText along with more interpretability. Our code and complete figures are available at https://github.com/LyzanderAndrylie/language-specific-features

papers.title: Layer Swapping for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Transfer in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we facilitate cross-lingual transfer of mathematical reasoning capabilities to non-English languages without in-language math data by merging models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces layer swapping, a model merging method that swaps top and bottom transformer layers from a language expert into a math expert to enable zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of mathematical reasoning without in-language task data.
papers.conclusion: Layer swapping is an effective, flexible, and inexpensive method for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of reasoning capabilities, with potential for broader application in multilingual LLM development.
papers.key_findings:
Layer swapping outperforms individual experts and model souping on the MGSM benchmark by an average of 10% across four languages (Swahili, Telugu, Bengali, Japanese).
Analysis of fine-tuning updates shows math capabilities are concentrated in middle transformer layers, while language capabilities are in the top and bottom layers.
The method is simple, inexpensive, and fully post hoc, requiring no further training or in-language task data.
The method provides the biggest benefit for lower-resource languages where cross-lingual transfer during standard fine-tuning is limited.
Transition zones between swapped layers were not necessary in the tested setting but are included as a component of the methodology.
papers.limitation:
The method was only evaluated on one model size (LLAMA 3.1 8B) and a limited set of languages and tasks (mathematical reasoning).
The experts were not fine-tuned for very long, which may affect the need for transition zones and the generalizability of the findings.
future_direction: Testing the method with frozen parameters from the start of training.
Applying layer swapping to LLMs with different pretraining distributions (e.g., balanced multilingual pretraining).
Extending the method to other reasoning tasks, parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings, and different training stages.
papers.abstract: Model merging, such as model souping, is the practice of combining different models with the same architecture together without further training. In this work, we present a model merging methodology that addresses the difficulty of fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) for target tasks in non-English languages, where task-specific data is often unavailable. We focus on mathematical reasoning and without in-language math data, facilitate cross-lingual transfer by composing language and math capabilities. Starting from the same pretrained model, we fine-tune separate "experts" on math instruction data in English and on generic instruction data in the target language. We then replace the top and bottom transformer layers of the math expert directly with layers from the language expert, which consequently enhances math performance in the target language. The resulting merged models outperform the individual experts and other merging methods on the math benchmark, MGSM, by 10% across four major languages where math instruction data is scarce. In addition, this layer swapping is simple, inexpensive, and intuitive, as it is based on an interpretative analysis of the most important parameter changes during the fine-tuning of each expert. The ability to successfully re-compose LLMs for cross-lingual transfer in this manner opens up future possibilities to combine model expertise, create modular solutions, and transfer reasoning capabilities across languages all post hoc.

papers.title: Exploring Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation: Mutual Opportunities and Open Challenges
papers.research_question: Can LLMs leverage both their robust capabilities (in English) and their multilingual knowledge (in non-English languages) during inference to further unlock their multilingual potential?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-lingual Latent Transplantation (X Transplant), a probing framework that transplants latent activations across languages at inference time to unlock multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs, revealing underutilized potential.
papers.conclusion: The analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
X Transplant has mutually beneficial effects on multilingual capability and cultural adaptability, especially for low-resource languages and cultures.
Attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge.
The upper-bound performance of X Transplant reveals a significant underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential.
English boosts multilingual capability, while non-English improves cultural adaptability.
papers.abstract: Current large language models (LLMs) often exhibit imbalances in multilingual capabilities and cultural adaptability, largely attributed to their English-centric pre-training data. In this paper, we introduce and investigate a cross-lingual latent transplantation (XTransplant) framework, which aims to further exploit the model's internalized multilingual knowledge during inference and examine its effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs. XTransplant framework enables models to harness the complementary strengths of both English and non-English resources by transplanting latent activations across languages. Through extensive analysis, we empirically demonstrate that XTransplant, a form of cross-lingual interaction, has mutually beneficial effects on the multilingual capability and cultural adaptability of LLMs, particularly for low-resource languages and cultures. We further reveal that attention modules play a pivotal role in supporting multilingual understanding, while feed-forward modules are more adept at capturing culture-specific knowledge. In addition, we conduct in-depth analysis of XTransplant's stability, effectiveness, and generalizability. By probing the upper bound performance of XTransplant, we expose the considerable underutilization of current LLMs' multilingual potential-a challenge that remains open. We hope our analysis offers a new lens for advancing cross-lingual interactions and better leveraging models' internalized multilingual knowledge.

papers.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning in Transformers work? The paper hypothesizes that Transformers implement gradient descent in their forward pass to learn from in-context data.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers trained on auto-regressive objectives implement gradient descent in their forward pass, providing a mechanistic understanding of in-context learning for regression tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning in Transformers can be understood as gradient descent in the forward pass, at least for regression tasks, providing a mechanistic understanding.
papers.key_findings:
A single linear self-attention layer can be constructed to perform one step of gradient descent on a linear regression loss.
When trained on linear regression tasks, linear self-attention-only Transformers converge to weights that match the gradient descent construction.
Multiple layers of self-attention can implement multiple steps of gradient descent and even surpass plain gradient descent by learning a curvature correction (GD++).
Transformers with MLPs can solve nonlinear regression tasks by learning linear models on deep representations.
The paper connects the induction head mechanism to in-context learning by gradient descent.
papers.limitation:
The findings on linear self-attention-only Transformers only explain a limited part of a complex process, and it may be one of many possible methods giving rise to in-context learning.
The analysis is limited to regression tasks and simple Transformer architectures.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to language modeling and other domains.
Investigating the role of softmax and LayerNorm in in-context learning.
Exploring the connection to hypernetworks and weight generation.
papers.abstract: At present, the mechanisms of in-context learning in Transformers are not well understood and remain mostly an intuition. In this paper, we suggest that training Transformers on auto-regressive objectives is closely related to gradient-based meta-learning formulations. We start by providing a simple weight construction that shows the equivalence of data transformations induced by 1) a single linear self-attention layer and by 2) gradient-descent (GD) on a regression loss. Motivated by that construction, we show empirically that when training self-attention-only Transformers on simple regression tasks either the models learned by GD and Transformers show great similarity or, remarkably, the weights found by optimization match the construction. Thus we show how trained Transformers become mesa-optimizers i.e. learn models by gradient descent in their forward pass. This allows us, at least in the domain of regression problems, to mechanistically understand the inner workings of in-context learning in optimized Transformers. Building on this insight, we furthermore identify how Transformers surpass the performance of plain gradient descent by learning an iterative curvature correction and learn linear models on deep data representations to solve non-linear regression tasks. Finally, we discuss intriguing parallels to a mechanism identified to be crucial for in-context learning termed induction-head (Olsson et al., 2022) and show how it could be understood as a specific case of in-context learning by gradient descent learning within Transformers. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at https://github.com/google-research/self-organising-systems/tree/master/transformers_learn_icl_by_gd .

papers.title: A Shared Geometry of Difficulty in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether problem-difficulty representations in multilingual LLMs are language-specific or shared across languages, and how they are encoded depth-dependently.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode problem difficulty in a depth-dependent manner: early layers form a language-agnostic representation that supports cross-lingual transfer, while deeper layers refine it into language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form a language-agnostic estimate of difficulty in early layers before specializing it to individual languages in deeper layers, indicating a shared geometry of difficulty across languages.
papers.key_findings:
Difficulty is linearly decodable from both shallow (early) and deep (later) transformer layers.
Probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages than those trained on deep representations.
Probes trained on deep representations achieve higher accuracy within the same language but generalize poorly across languages.
There is a trade-off between cross-lingual generalization and language-specific accuracy, with optimal layers differing for same-language vs. cross-lingual evaluation.
This depth-dependent organization of difficulty representations is consistent across multiple LLM architectures and scales.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is confined to mathematical problem solving using the AMC subset of Easy2Hard, so it is unclear if findings extend to other domains.
Empirical evaluation is limited to a small set of instruction-tuned, decoder-only language models.
Conclusions are based exclusively on probing analyses without causal evidence for the role of difficulty signals in inference.
future_direction: Whether difficulty-based interventions learned in one language transfer to other languages.
papers.abstract: Predicting problem-difficulty in large language models (LLMs) refers to estimating how difficult a task is according to the model itself, typically by training linear probes on its internal representations. In this work, we study the multilingual geometry of problem-difficulty in LLMs by training linear probes using the AMC subset of the Easy2Hard benchmark, translated into 21 languages. We found that difficulty-related signals emerge at two distinct stages of the model internals, corresponding to shallow (early-layers) and deep (later-layers) internal representations, that exhibit functionally different behaviors. Probes trained on deep representations achieve high accuracy when evaluated on the same language but exhibit poor cross-lingual generalization. In contrast, probes trained on shallow representations generalize substantially better across languages, despite achieving lower within-language performance. Together, these results suggest that LLMs first form a language-agnostic representation of problem difficulty, which subsequently becomes language-specific. This closely aligns with existing findings in LLM interpretability showing that models tend to operate in an abstract conceptual space before producing language-specific outputs. We demonstrate that this two-stage representational process extends beyond semantic content to high-level meta-cognitive properties such as problem-difficulty estimation.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual large language models develop a universal interlingua representation, or present a partially aligned construct toward certain languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework and the Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) metric to analyze interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs, and shows that selectively freezing early layers during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and improves cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Interlingual semantic alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning, and the proposed framework and ILO metric provide effective tools for evaluating and preserving this alignment in multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments, with stronger alignment between high-resource languages and within the same linguistic family or region.
Single-language fine-tuning disrupts interlingual alignment, particularly in early layers, leading to degraded cross-lingual generalization.
Selectively freezing early layers (and other alignment-critical parameters) during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and significantly improves cross-lingual transfer performance.
The proposed ILO score effectively quantifies the degree of interlingual alignment by measuring the local neighborhood structure of high-dimensional representations.
Interlingual overlaps that transcend familial and regional boundaries are observed in intermediate model layers, while early and late layers show clustering by resource level and linguistic features.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on massive multilingual datasets hint at the formation of interlingual constructs--a shared subspace in the representation space. However, evidence regarding this phenomenon is mixed, leaving it unclear whether these models truly develop unified interlingual representations, or present a partially aligned constructs. We explore 31 diverse languages varying on their resource-levels, typologies, and geographical regions; and find that multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments. To address this, we propose an interlingual representation framework identifying both the shared interlingual semantic subspace and fragmented components, existed due to representational limitations. We introduce Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) score to quantify interlingual alignment by comparing the local neighborhood structures of high-dimensional representations. We utilize ILO to investigate the impact of single-language fine-tuning on the interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs. Our results indicate that training exclusively on a single language disrupts the alignment in early layers, while freezing these layers preserves the alignment of interlingual representations, leading to improved cross-lingual generalization. These results validate our framework and metric for evaluating interlingual representation, and further underscore that interlingual alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning.

papers.title: Pretraining with Artificial Language: Studying Transferable Knowledge in Language Models
papers.research_question: What kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language?
papers.core_contribution: Pretraining with an artificial language that has a nesting dependency structure provides transferable knowledge to natural language tasks, and the transferred knowledge is related to position-aware context dependence.
papers.conclusion: The transferable knowledge in pretrained encoders can be characterized as position-aware context dependence, meaning tokens in a sequence can be characterized by their neighbor tokens at specific positions.
papers.key_findings:
Pretraining with an artificial language that models statistical dependency within a sentence (Log-linear) provides a useful inductive bias for natural language modeling.
A nesting head-to-tail dependency structure is more beneficial for transfer than a flat structure.
Encoders pretrained on languages with nesting dependency structures are better at capturing local contextual information, which is important for tasks like dependency parsing.
The amount of contextual information encoded by the pretrained encoder (as measured by a probing task) correlates with its transfer performance in some cases.
The Uniform and Zipf languages, which lack token dependencies, degrade encoder performance compared to random initialization.
papers.limitation: The knowledge of position-aware context dependence may not explain every aspect of the success of cross-lingual transfer.
future_direction: Investigate how model size affects the transferability of the encoder.
Investigate if there is any difference in the knowledge transferred among different downstream tasks.
papers.abstract: We investigate what kind of structural knowledge learned in neural network encoders is transferable to processing natural language. We design artificial languages with structural properties that mimic natural language, pretrain encoders on the data, and see how much performance the encoder exhibits on downstream tasks in natural language. Our experimental results show that pretraining with an artificial language with a nesting dependency structure provides some knowledge transferable to natural language. A follow-up probing analysis indicates that its success in the transfer is related to the amount of encoded contextual information and what is transferred is the knowledge of position-aware context dependence of language. Our results provide insights into how neural network encoders process human languages and the source of cross-lingual transferability of recent multilingual language models.

papers.title: Lost in Multilinguality: Dissecting Cross-lingual Factual Inconsistency in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the underlying causes of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models, and how can this inconsistency be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that cross-lingual factual inconsistency in multilingual language models arises from failures in the language transition phase in the final layers, and proposes a linear shortcut method that bypasses these layers to improve both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
papers.conclusion: Language transition errors are a key cause of cross-lingual inconsistency, and the proposed linear shortcut method effectively mitigates this issue, improving model consistency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual language models encode factual knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, transitioning to language-specific spaces only in the final layers.
Incorrect predictions in the target language often occur due to failures during the language transition, even when the correct answer is present in the concept space.
The proposed linear shortcut method, which bypasses final-layer computations, enhances prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency.
The concept space in LLaMA2 is English-centric, while BLOOM's concept space is more linguistically diverse.
The knowledge recall process in multilingual models involves three stages: relation processing, object extraction in the latent language, and language-specific adaptation.
papers.limitation:
The analysis assumes English as the pivot language, which may limit applicability to language pairs that do not involve English.
The KLAR dataset covers 17 languages but does not fully capture the diversity of world languages.
The shortcut method relies on linear approximation; non-linear approaches might better capture complex transformations.
The study does not explore downstream applications such as multilingual knowledge localization or editing.
future_direction: Expand the investigation to more languages and additional language models to assess broader applicability.
Develop non-linear shortcut methods to better mitigate language transition errors.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models (MLMs) store factual knowledge across languages but often struggle to provide consistent responses to semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While previous studies point out this cross-lingual inconsistency issue, the underlying causes remain unexplored. In this work, we use mechanistic interpretability methods to investigate cross-lingual inconsistencies in MLMs. We find that MLMs encode knowledge in a language-independent concept space through most layers, and only transition to language-specific spaces in the final layers. Failures during the language transition often result in incorrect predictions in the target language, even when the answers are correct in other languages. To mitigate this inconsistency issue, we propose a linear shortcut method that bypasses computations in the final layers, enhancing both prediction accuracy and cross-lingual consistency. Our findings shed light on the internal mechanisms of MLMs and provide a lightweight, effective strategy for producing more consistent factual outputs.

papers.title: Cross-Lingual Activation Steering for Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How can inference-time neuron activation steering improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual language models without additional training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time method that modulates neuron activations to improve cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by rebalancing shared and language-specific representations.
papers.conclusion: CLAS effectively improves cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LLMs by steering activations to promote functional divergence, with gains not reliant on geometric alignment to the anchor language.
papers.key_findings:
CLAS achieves average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) on classification and generation benchmarks, respectively.
Performance improvements are driven by functional divergence, with gains correlating with increased language cluster separation rather than closer alignment to English.
CLAS reduces cosine similarity to English for non-anchor languages, indicating a shift away from strict geometric alignment.
Qualitative analysis shows CLAS suppresses repetition loops and verbosity in generation outputs.
The steering parameter alpha can be positive or negative for optimal performance, indicating task- and model-dependent balance between shared and language-specific signals.
papers.limitation:
Analysis and intervention are anchored to English, which may not generalize to other anchor languages.
CLAS is not uniformly beneficial and can cause performance regressions for some languages.
Mechanistic analysis does not isolate attention heads or other circuit components, limiting causal attribution.
future_direction: Explore adaptive steering strategies based on representational structure.
Better understand saturation effects in well-separated language clusters.
Extend CLAS to other modalities and training settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit strong multilingual capabilities, yet significant performance gaps persist between dominant and non-dominant languages. Prior work attributes this gap to imbalances between shared and language-specific neurons in multilingual representations. We propose Cross-Lingual Activation Steering (CLAS), a training-free inference-time intervention that selectively modulates neuron activations. We evaluate CLAS on classification and generation benchmarks, achieving average improvements of 2.3% (Acc.) and 3.4% (F1) respectively, while maintaining high-resource language performance. We discover that effective transfer operates through functional divergence rather than strict alignment; performance gains correlate with increased language cluster separation. Our results demonstrate that targeted activation steering can unlock latent multilingual capacity in existing models without modification to model weights.

papers.title: A multilabel approach to morphosyntactic probing
papers.research_question: How well does multilingual BERT encode morphosyntactic features across languages, and which features are recognized as shared cross-linguistically?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a multilabel probing paradigm for morphosyntactic analysis and demonstrates that multilingual BERT encodes many morphosyntactic features extractably, with some features shared cross-linguistically.
papers.conclusion: Multilabel probing is an effective method for analyzing morphosyntactic representations in multilingual language models, revealing that mBERT encodes many features and that some are represented cross-linguistically.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT-6 holds the most morphosyntactic information, with probes achieving micro-averaged F1 scores between 0.83 and 0.97 for seven languages.
Multilingual probes slightly underperform monolingual probes but exhibit better selectivity, suggesting less memorization.
Cross-lingual transfer experiments show that nouns and verbs are well transferred, while adjectives and nominative case are less consistently recognized across languages.
The multilabel paradigm enables fine-grained analysis of feature co-occurrence and agreement patterns, as demonstrated in a case study of Hebrew determiners.
Probe performance varies across languages due to differences in feature sets and training set sizes, making direct comparison difficult.
papers.limitation: The UD corpora used are from narrow domains (e.g., Wikipedia, news, Bible) and may not capture the full range of linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Probe different multilingual language models to compare their morphosyntactic representations.
Explore how global and feature-level probe performance corresponds to downstream task performance.
Conduct more detailed analyses of specific features and their cross-linguistic transfer.
papers.abstract: We propose using a multilabel probing task to assess the morphosyntactic representations of multilingual word embeddings. This tweak on canonical probing makes it easy to explore morphosyntactic representations, both holistically and at the level of individual features (e.g., gender, number, case), and leads more naturally to the study of how language models handle co-occurring features (e.g., agreement phenomena). We demonstrate this task with multilingual BERT Through this simple but robust paradigm, we verify that multilingual BERT renders many morphosyntactic features simultaneously extractable. We further evaluate the probes on six held-out languages: Arabic, Chinese, Marathi, Slovenian, Tagalog, and Yorb. This zero-shot style of probing has the added benefit of revealing which cross-linguistic properties a language model recognizes as being shared by multiple languages.

papers.title: Similarity of Sentence Representations in Multilingual LMs: Resolving Conflicting Literature and Case Study of Baltic Languages
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the conflicting conclusions in prior work about cross-lingual representations in multilingual LMs and aims to determine the correct pattern and the best practices for analysis, with a case study on Baltic languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper resolves conflicting literature on cross-lingual representations in multilingual LMs by showing that the choice of pooling strategy (mean-pooling over CLS-pooling) and similarity index (CKA/SVCCA over PWCCA) is critical, and that most languages, including Baltic languages, share a joint cross-lingual space in middle layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mean-pooling with SVCCA/CKA is the most suitable choice for cross-lingual representational similarity analysis, that this pattern is present in other multilingual LMs, and that while not all languages share the cross-lingual space equally, Baltic languages do.
papers.key_findings:
The divergence pattern reported by Singh et al. (2019) is an artifact of using CLS-pooling with PWCCA; using mean-pooling with CKA or SVCCA reveals a convergence pattern as reported by Muller et al. (2021).
CLS-pooling provides poor semantic representations for cross-lingual analysis in early layers, while mean-pooling performs better.
Mean-pooling with CKA or SVCCA is the recommended method for cross-lingual representational similarity analysis.
The convergence pattern generalizes across most languages in mBERT and XLM-R, but some languages (e.g., Urdu, Hindi, Swahili, Thai) are outliers and do not share the joint cross-lingual space.
Baltic languages (Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian) belong to the shared cross-lingual space and cluster together meaningfully.
future_direction: Finding the exact criteria for exclusion from the shared cross-lingual space is left for future work.
papers.abstract: Low-resource languages, such as Baltic languages, benefit from Large Multilingual Models (LMs) that possess remarkable cross-lingual transfer performance capabilities. This work is an interpretation and analysis study into cross-lingual representations of Multilingual LMs. Previous works hypothesized that these LMs internally project representations of different languages into a shared cross-lingual space. However, the literature produced contradictory results. In this paper, we revisit the prior work claiming that "BERT is not an Interlingua" and show that different languages do converge to a shared space in such language models with another choice of pooling strategy or similarity index. Then, we perform cross-lingual representational analysis for the two most popular multilingual LMs employing 378 pairwise language comparisons. We discover that while most languages share joint cross-lingual space, some do not. However, we observe that Baltic languages do belong to that shared space. The code is available at https://github.com/TartuNLP/xsim.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Just-in-time and distributed task representations in language models
papers.research_question: When are transferrable task representations formed in language models during in-context learning, and how do they change over the context?
papers.core_contribution: Transferrable task representations in language models evolve non-monotonically and sporadically, activating only at key tokens, while a persistent representation of task identity is maintained throughout the context.
papers.conclusion: Language models form multiple types of task representations during in-context learning, with transferrable representations activating sporadically and task identity persisting, revealing a complex and nuanced dynamic of the model's internal state.
papers.key_findings:
Transferrable task representations (e.g., task vectors) accrue evidence from multiple in-context examples but form sporadically and non-monotonically.
Task identity representations are robustly decodable from residual activations across most tokens in the context, persisting throughout.
Transferrable task representations exhibit strong temporal locality, forming effectively only at specific tokens (e.g., the colon token before answer generation).
In longer- and mixed-generation tasks, transferrable task representations often decay over output units, showing semantic locality and limited task scope.
For complex tasks requiring state tracking or combining distinct subtasks, effective task representations are more distributed across tokens.
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot recontextualization remains challenging for tasks that require intermediate-state tracking or more complicated computation.
Overriding token activations at intermediate layers with task vectors may cause the model to lose task state information formed in earlier layers.
future_direction: Study the mechanistic bases for the strong temporal and scope locality observed in models' in-context transferrable task representations.
papers.abstract: Many of language models' impressive capabilities originate from their in-context learning: based on instructions or examples, they can infer and perform new tasks without weight updates. In this work, we investigate when representations for new tasks are formed in language models, and how these representations change over the course of context. We study two different task representations: those that are ''transferrable'' -- vector representations that can transfer task contexts to another model instance, even without the full prompt -- and simpler representations of high-level task categories. We show that transferrable task representations evolve in non-monotonic and sporadic ways, while task identity representations persist throughout the context. Specifically, transferrable task representations exhibit a two-fold locality. They successfully condense evidence when more examples are provided in the context.
