papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LINSPECTOR, a set of multilingual probing tasks and an evaluation suite for word representations, and shows that probing task performance correlates with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the introduced probing tasks and the LINSPECTOR framework are effective for evaluating word representations in multiple languages and that they correlate with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.key_findings:
Probing tasks can be used to evaluate word embeddings in multiple languages and show significant positive correlation with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
All embedding models achieved their lowest score for CharacterBin, a task that requires predicting the number of characters.
D-ELMo achieves the highest scores in probing for all language-test pairs, generally followed by fastText and GloVe-BPE.
Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
The probing tasks can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting.
papers.limitation: Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
future_direction: Extend probing tasks to more languages and include more linguistic phenomena.
Investigate the use of probing tasks for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Despite an ever-growing number of word representation models introduced for a large number of languages, there is a lack of a standardized technique to provide insights into what is captured by these models. Such insights would help the community to get an estimate of the downstream task performance, as well as to design more informed neural architectures, while avoiding extensive experimentation that requires substantial computational resources not all researchers have access to. A recent development in NLP is to use simple classification tasks, also called probing tasks, that test for a single linguistic feature such as part-of-speech. Existing studies mostly focus on exploring the linguistic information encoded by the continuous representations of English text. However, from a typological perspective the morphologically poor English is rather an outlier: The information encoded by the word order and function words in English is often stored on a subword, morphological level in other languages. To address this, we introduce 15 type-level probing tasks such as case marking, possession, word length, morphological tag count, and pseudoword identification for 24 languages. We present a reusable methodology for creation and evaluation of such tests in a multilingual setting, which is challenging because of a lack of resources, lower quality of tools, and differences among languages. We then present experiments on several diverse multilingual word embedding models, in which we relate the probing task performance for a diverse set of languages to a range of five classic NLP tasks: POS-tagging, dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, named entity recognition, and natural language inference. We find that a number of probing tests have significantly high positive correlation to the downstream tasks, especially for morphologically rich languages. We show that our tests can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting. We release the probing data sets and the evaluation suite LINSPECTOR with https://github.com/UKPLab/linspector .

papers.title: Unraveling Arithmetic in Large Language Models: The Role of Algebraic Structures
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) learn to perform arithmetic operations? Specifically, do they capture underlying algebraic structures like commutativity and identity from input-output relationships?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes that LLMs learn arithmetic by capturing algebraic structures such as commutativity and identity from input-output relationships, rather than by directly encoding numerical values. It provides both empirical evidence using custom datasets and a theoretical construction showing transformer-based models can be configured to exhibit invariance to input permutations and identity element insertion.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can internalize algebraic structures like commutativity and identity from training data, providing a foundation for understanding and potentially enhancing their arithmetic capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can learn and generalize the commutative and identity properties of operators from training data to unseen inputs.
The learning is operator-specific; models can distinguish between operators that have these properties (like '+') and those that do not (like '⊖').
Performance on a synthetic operator '⊕' shows that LLMs learn these algebraic structures without relying on underlying numerical calculations of the input indices.
Learning commutativity requires a larger training set size than learning identity or non-commutative operators, but the required size is still much smaller than the full combinatorial space.
All tested tasks, including learning commutative and identity properties for '+' and '⊕' and learning non-commutative operators '⊖', '⊳', and '⊲', eventually achieve over 99% testing accuracy with sufficient training data.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable mathematical capabilities, largely driven by chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, which decomposes complex reasoning into step-by-step solutions. This approach has enabled significant advancements, as evidenced by performance on benchmarks like GSM8K and MATH. However, the mechanisms underlying LLMs' ability to perform arithmetic in a single step of CoT remain poorly understood. Existing studies debate whether LLMs encode numerical values or rely on symbolic reasoning, while others explore attention and multi-layered processing in arithmetic tasks. In this work, we propose that LLMs learn arithmetic by capturing algebraic structures, such as commutativity and identity properties. Since these structures are observable through input-output relationships, they can generalize to unseen data. We empirically demonstrate that LLMs can learn algebraic structures using a custom dataset of arithmetic problems, as well as providing theoretical evidence showing that, under specific configurations of weights and biases, the transformer-based LLMs can generate embeddings that remain invariant to both permutations of input tokens and the presence of identity elements. Our findings indicate that leveraging algebraic structures can enhance the LLMs' arithmetic capabilities, offering insights into improving their arithmetic performance.

papers.title: Deep Subjecthood: Higher-Order Grammatical Features in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: How does Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encode abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment, and is subjecthood represented as a discrete or continuous category?
papers.core_contribution: mBERT encodes high-level grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by semantic and discourse factors.
papers.conclusion: mBERT encodes abstract grammatical features like morphosyntactic alignment in its contextual embeddings, and subjecthood is represented as a continuous, probabilistic concept influenced by both syntax and semantics.
papers.key_findings:
Classifiers trained to distinguish transitive subjects (A) and objects (O) from mBERT embeddings achieve high accuracy, peaking in middle layers (7-10).
When tested on intransitive subjects (S), classifier predictions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of the training language: classifiers trained on ergative languages are more likely to classify S as O.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of subjecthood classification is successful, indicating parallel encoding of grammatical relations across languages in mBERT.
Classifier decisions are influenced by semantic and syntactic factors: passive subjects are ambiguous, animate nouns are more likely to be classified as agents, and case markings affect classification.
mBERT's representation of subjecthood is continuous and probabilistic, aligning with functional linguistics theories rather than being a purely discrete syntactic category.
papers.limitation: The Universal Dependencies training data and mBERT training languages are heavily weighted towards nominative-accusative languages, leading to a nominative-accusative bias and noisy results due to limited ergative language data.
future_direction: Examine the effects of balanced joint training between nominative-accusative and ergative-absolutive languages on the contextual embedding of subjecthood.
Continue investigating how deep neural models represent discrete linguistic features probabilistically.
papers.abstract: We investigate how Multilingual BERT (mBERT) encodes grammar by examining how the high-order grammatical feature of morphosyntactic alignment (how different languages define what counts as a "subject") is manifested across the embedding spaces of different languages. To understand if and how morphosyntactic alignment affects contextual embedding spaces, we train classifiers to recover the subjecthood of mBERT embeddings in transitive sentences (which do not contain overt information about morphosyntactic alignment) and then evaluate them zero-shot on intransitive sentences (where subjecthood classification depends on alignment), within and across languages. We find that the resulting classifier distributions reflect the morphosyntactic alignment of their training languages. Our results demonstrate that mBERT representations are influenced by high-level grammatical features that are not manifested in any one input sentence, and that this is robust across languages. Further examining the characteristics that our classifiers rely on, we find that features such as passive voice, animacy and case strongly correlate with classification decisions, suggesting that mBERT does not encode subjecthood purely syntactically, but that subjecthood embedding is continuous and dependent on semantic and discourse factors, as is proposed in much of the functional linguistics literature. Together, these results provide insight into how grammatical features manifest in contextual embedding spaces, at a level of abstraction not covered by previous work.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: How do languages influence each other? Studying cross-lingual data sharing during LM fine-tuning
papers.research_question: To what extent, and under which conditions, do multilingual language models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the use of Training Data Attribution (TDA) methods, specifically TracIn, to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level in multilingual language models, finding that models rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that languages largely influence one another cross-lingually under various conditions, with cross-lingual sharing increasing during fine-tuning and languages playing both reinforcing and complementary roles.
papers.key_findings:
MLMs rely on data from multiple languages during fine-tuning and this reliance increases as fine-tuning progresses.
Training samples from other languages can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.
The model exhibits different cross-lingual behaviour in zero-shot testing compared to when the test language is seen during fine-tuning.
Even with data imbalances, the model largely benefits from cross-lingual sharing.
For parallel datasets, cross-lingual sharing is high, and for non-parallel datasets, it is still observed but to a lesser extent.
papers.limitation:
Computational expense limited the study to 125 test samples.
The method is restricted to relatively easy classification tasks and not generation or sequence labeling tasks.
The analysis focuses on the fine-tuning stage and does not disentangle pre-training effects.
future_direction: Extending influence function methods to sequence tagging tasks for more fine-grained analysis.
Studying the emergence of cross-lingual abilities during pre-training.
Inspiring future work on studying sharing mechanisms within multi-task and multi-modal models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) are jointly trained on data from many different languages such that representation of individual languages can benefit from other languages' data. Impressive performance on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer shows that these models are capable of exploiting data from other languages. Yet, it remains unclear to what extent, and under which conditions, languages rely on each other's data. In this study, we use TracIn (Pruthi et al., 2020), a training data attribution (TDA) method, to retrieve the most influential training samples seen during multilingual fine-tuning for a particular test language. This allows us to analyse cross-lingual sharing mechanisms of MLLMs from a new perspective. While previous work studied cross-lingual sharing at the level of model parameters, we present the first approach to study cross-lingual sharing at the data level. We find that MLLMs rely on data from multiple languages from the early stages of fine-tuning and that this reliance gradually increases as fine-tuning progresses. We further study how different fine-tuning languages influence model performance on a given test language and find that they can both reinforce and complement the knowledge acquired from data of the test language itself.

papers.title: On the Linguistic Representational Power of Neural Machine Translation Models
papers.research_question: How do neural machine translation models capture linguistic information (morphology, syntax, semantics) in their representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that neural machine translation models learn non-trivial linguistic information in their representations, with a hierarchical organization: lower layers capture local, low-level properties (morphology) and higher layers capture global, high-level properties (syntax, semantics).
papers.conclusion: Deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without direct supervision, learn a substantial amount of linguistic information, and the representations are organized in a hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model.
Lexical semantics and non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model.
Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units.
Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.
The target language impacts the kind of information learned by the MT system, with translation into morphologically-poorer languages leading to better source-side word representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language processing and other spheres of artificial intelligence, their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the representations learned by neural machine translation (NMT) models at various levels of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How accurately is word structure captured within the learned representations, which is an important aspect in translating morphologically rich languages? (ii) Do the representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i) Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena; (ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit) impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations? (iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven, quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without being provided any direct supervision during the training process, learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include the following observations: (i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model; (iii) Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: Language-Specific Neurons: The Key to Multilingual Capabilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models process multilingual texts, and can we identify language-specific neurons that are key to their multilingual capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language activation probability entropy (LAPE) to identify language-specific neurons in LLMs, and finds that a small subset of neurons in the top and bottom layers is crucial for multilingual processing, enabling steering of output language.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces LAPE to identify language-specific neurons, finds that a small subset of neurons in top/bottom layers are key to multilingual processing, and demonstrates that output language can be steered by manipulating these neurons.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of neurons (identified by LAPE) is crucial for processing a particular language; deactivating them severely degrades performance in that language.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in the top and bottom layers of the transformer, with bottom layers mapping to a shared semantic space and top layers mapping to language-specific vocabulary.
Larger models tend to have neurons specialized for single languages, while smaller models may share neurons across languages.
Chinese and Japanese share many language-specific neurons, likely due to character overlap.
Selectively activating or deactivating language-specific neurons can steer the output language of the model, mitigating off-target language issues.
papers.limitation:
The method is relative to the presence of multiple languages and cannot establish an absolute threshold for single-language scenarios.
The criteria for distinguishing high-resource and low-resource languages need further investigation.
The research only begins to explore steering output language; strategies to enhance multilingual proficiency are still needed.
future_direction: Enhance knowledge transfer between major and minor languages.
Devise efficient strategies for continual pre-training to better accommodate specific languages.
Investigate the model's ability to manage a large number of languages and the differences between languages.
papers.abstract: Tianyi Tang, Wenyang Luo, Haoyang Huang, Dongdong Zhang, Xiaolei Wang, Xin Zhao, Furu Wei, Ji-Rong Wen. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations
papers.research_question: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? Which typological features can be discovered when the system is not told what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that neural models can sometimes learn typological generalizations in their language representations, but less readily than suggested by prior work, and that careful evaluation is essential to avoid false positives. It also releases several resources for 1295 languages.
papers.conclusion: Neural models can discover typological generalizations, but they do so less readily than suggested by previous research, and careful evaluation is necessary to confirm such discoveries.
papers.key_findings:
Some generalizations in learned language representations are surprisingly close to traditional typological features, but most models (including those from previous work) do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations.
Careful attention to evaluation details, such as controlling for genealogical and areal correlations, is essential to avoid false positives.
The word-level language model (WordLM) captures word order features and some morphological features, while many other models (including MTVec, MTCell, and Ö&T) show little evidence of encoding typological features when evaluated with their method.
Lexical baselines (ASJP and Lexical similarity vectors) do not encode structural features, as expected, and can serve as a baseline for evaluation.
papers.limitation: The study only tries to connect neural language representations with known features from the typological literature, not with potentially novel generalizations.
future_direction: Investigating whether models make typological generalizations that human linguists have not previously made.
papers.abstract: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? We explore these questions by training neural models for a range of natural language processing tasks on a massively multilingual dataset of Bible translations in 1295 languages. The learned language representations are then compared to existing typological databases as well as to a novel set of quantitative syntactic and morphological features obtained through annotation projection. We conclude that some generalizations are surprisingly close to traditional features from linguistic typology, but that most of our models, as well as those of previous work, do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations. Careful attention to details in the evaluation turns out to be essential to avoid false positives. Furthermore, to encourage continued work in this field, we release several resources covering most or all of the languages in our data: (i) multiple sets of language representations, (ii) multilingual word embeddings, (iii) projected and predicted syntactic and morphological features, (iv) software to provide linguistically sound evaluations of language representations.

papers.title: Exploring Representational Disparities Between Multilingual and Bilingual Translation Models
papers.research_question: How does the ambient space utilization of model representations differ between bilingual models and one-to-many models? If space utilization differs, what might be driving these differences?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than bilingual decoder representations, largely due to language-specific information occupying representational capacity.
papers.conclusion: There is a consistent reduction in representational capacity in multilingual decoders versus bilingual decoders, attributed to language information occupying a significant portion of the representation space.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual decoder representations are less isotropic than bilingual decoder representations across different data resource levels and language pairs.
Multilingual encoder representations are slightly more isotropic than bilingual encoder representations, but the improvement is smaller than the decoder reduction.
The reduction in multilingual decoder isotropy is driven by language-specific information occupying much of the available representation space.
Isotropy decreases with larger training scale, related to the representation degeneration problem.
In multiparallel data, the decoder isotropy reduction is less pronounced for related languages (e.g., Russian and Ukrainian).
papers.limitation:
Models cover at most 3 language families, while modern multilingual translation models cover many more.
Focus on one-to-many models, but many-to-many models may have different behavior.
Focus on encoder-decoder models, but decoder-only translation models may differ.
Work focuses on characterization, not on improving representational capacity.
future_direction: Analyze models with larger language coverage.
Investigate many-to-many multilingual models.
Study decoder-only translation models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual machine translation has proven immensely useful for both parameter efficiency and overall performance across many language pairs via complete multilingual parameter sharing. However, some language pairs in multilingual models can see worse performance than in bilingual models, especially in the one-to-many translation setting. Motivated by their empirical differences, we examine the geometric differences in representations from bilingual models versus those from one-to-many multilingual models. Specifically, we compute the isotropy of these representations using intrinsic dimensionality and IsoScore, in order to measure how the representations utilize the dimensions in their underlying vector space. Using the same evaluation data in both models, we find that for a given language pair, its multilingual model decoder representations are consistently less isotropic and occupy fewer dimensions than comparable bilingual model decoder representations. Additionally, we show that much of the anisotropy in multilingual decoder representations can be attributed to modeling language-specific information, therefore limiting remaining representational capacity.

papers.title: Separating Tongue from Thought: Activation Patching Reveals Language-Agnostic Concept Representations in Transformers
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop universal concept representations that are disentangled from specific languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides causal evidence that transformer-based LLMs develop language-agnostic concept representations, as shown by activation patching experiments where averaging concept representations across languages improves translation performance.
papers.conclusion: Transformers use language-agnostic latent representations of concepts when processing word-level translation prompts, as evidenced by improved translation performance when averaging concept representations across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The model processes translation tasks by first resolving output language (layers 0-11), then the concept to be translated (layers 12-31).
Activation patching can independently manipulate language and concept information in the model's forward pass.
Patching with the mean representation of a concept across different languages improves translation performance, supporting language-agnostic representations.
These findings generalize across multiple transformer models of varying size, architecture, and training data.
The model can generate natural language descriptions of mean concept representations via activation patching.
papers.limitation: The study only considered simple concepts and did not investigate language-specific concepts.
future_direction: Improving cross-lingual transfer learning by leveraging shared concept spaces
More fine-grained probing to understand concept specialization to language
Reducing computational costs of multilingual training
papers.abstract: A central question in multilingual language modeling is whether large language models (LLMs) develop a universal concept representation, disentangled from specific languages. In this paper, we address this question by analyzing latent representations (latents) during a word-translation task in transformer-based LLMs. We strategically extract latents from a source translation prompt and insert them into the forward pass on a target translation prompt. By doing so, we find that the output language is encoded in the latent at an earlier layer than the concept to be translated. Building on this insight, we conduct two key experiments. First, we demonstrate that we can change the concept without changing the language and vice versa through activation patching alone. Second, we show that patching with the mean representation of a concept across different languages does not affect the models' ability to translate it, but instead improves it. Finally, we generalize to multi-token generation and demonstrate that the model can generate natural language description of those mean representations. Our results provide evidence for the existence of language-agnostic concept representations within the investigated models.

papers.title: Carrying over algorithm in transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition, and how are the tasks allocated to different network components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that transformer models implement the carrying over algorithm for integer addition in a modular fashion, with specific layers handling digit addition, carry decision, and carry addition.
papers.conclusion: Transformers implement the carrying over algorithm in a modular way, and insights from small models can inform understanding of larger models and improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
For two-layer encoder-only models, the carrying over algorithm is implemented modularly with the first layer adding digits, the second layer deciding where to carry, and the MLP adding the carried one.
The same implementation is found in three-layer and decoder-only models.
Suggestive evidence indicates similar mechanisms in large language models like Alpaca 7B, Llemma 7B, and Zephyr 7B.
Length generalization to larger digit sums can be achieved through priming or fine-tuning.
One-layer models exhibit a phase transition in attention patterns during training.
papers.limitation: The evidence for the implementation in large language models is suggestive and not conclusive.
future_direction: Exploring better prompting strategies for large language models
Studying stabilization of attention patterns for length generalization
papers.abstract: Addition is perhaps one of the simplest arithmetic tasks one can think of and is usually performed using the carrying over algorithm. This algorithm consists of two tasks: adding digits in the same position and carrying over a one whenever necessary. We study how transformer models implement this algorithm and how the two aforementioned tasks are allocated to different parts of the network. We first focus on two-layer encoder-only models and show that the carrying over algorithm is implemented in a modular fashion. The first layer is mostly responsible for adding digits in the same position. The second layer first decides, in the attention, which positions need a carried one or not, and then performs the carrying of the one in the final MLP. We provide a simple way of precisely identifying which neurons are responsible for that task. This implementation of the carrying over algorithm occurs across a range of hyperparameters for two as well as three-layer models. For small decoder-only models, we observe the same implementation and provide suggestive evidence for its existence in three 7B large language models.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we elicit latent knowledge from language models that are finetuned to make systematic errors, using probes on their activations?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes on middle-layer activations can extract context-independent knowledge from language models finetuned to output untruthfully, enabling elicitation of correct answers despite deceptive outputs.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that context-independent representations of knowledge exist in quirky models, and probing methods can reliably extract truth, informing scalable oversight of capable systems.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on truthful contexts generalize to untruthful contexts, indicating context-independent knowledge representations.
The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 75% of the performance gap between truthful and untruthful behavior on hard examples.
Mechanistic anomaly detection using Mahalanobis distance can flag untruthful behavior with an average AUROC of 0.95.
Difference-in-means probing directions are more causally implicated in model output and show better robustness to distribution shifts.
Unsupervised methods like CCS and CRC have an inductive bias towards context-independent generalization but achieve lower in-distribution performance.
papers.limitation:
Measurement of difficulty is a significant limitation, as different difficulty metrics are minimally correlated.
Contrast pair activations come from the answer token position, which is out-of-distribution for the finetuning data.
future_direction: Expand on the diversity and representativeness of evaluations by constructing new quirky datasets and models.
Investigate the limits of context-independent representations by varying the number of personas in finetuning.
Characterize the causal mechanisms involved, such as how intervening on knowledge representations affects output.
papers.abstract: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ELK) aims to find patterns in a capable neural network's activations that robustly track the true state of the world, especially in hard-to-verify cases where the model's output is untrusted. To further ELK research, we introduce 12 datasets and a corresponding suite of "quirky" language models (LMs) that are finetuned to make systematic errors when answering questions if and only if the keyword "Bob" is present in the prompt. We find that, especially in middle layers, linear probes usually report an LM's knowledge independently of what the LM outputs, enabling us to elicit the correct answer despite the model's untruthful output. The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC between truthful and untruthful contexts, and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe. We also find that a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC. Our results show promise for eliciting reliable knowledge from capable but untrusted models, and facilitates future research empirically investigating ELK methods.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Universal and Independent: Multilingual Probing Framework for Exhaustive Model Interpretation and Evaluation
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether the regularities detected in language models are linguistically coherent across typological diversity, and addresses the lack of coverage of typological diversity in existing probing studies.
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework for exhaustive multilingual probing covering 104 languages and 80 morphosyntactic features, and applies it to show that mBERT's learned regularities are biased towards Standard Average European languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents the Universal Probing framework for multilingual model interpretation and evaluation, demonstrating its use and revealing a bias in mBERT towards Standard Average European languages.
papers.key_findings:
The framework enables massive multilingual probing and aggregation of results.
mBERT and XLM-R show similar performance, with mBERT slightly better.
Models perform better on high-resource languages and worse on under-resourced non-Indo-European languages.
Model performance is correlated with language family but not with script.
Models are biased towards Standard Average European (SAE) languages, performing better on categories found in SAE languages.
papers.limitation:
The framework depends on Universal Dependencies data, which may contain annotation errors, formatting errors, and version instability.
The framework allows the use of widely criticized probing methods, requiring careful selection by researchers.
The dataset may have genre bias, personal style/resource bias, and collocation of features, making classification noisy.
The language set is not typologically sampled but based on completeness, potentially affecting representativeness.
future_direction: Including syntactic markup in research.
Developing an interface with a CQL-like query language for creating custom probing tasks.
papers.abstract: Linguistic analysis of language models is one of the ways to explain and describe their reasoning, weaknesses, and limitations. In the probing part of the model interpretability research, studies concern individual languages as well as individual linguistic structures. The question arises: are the detected regularities linguistically coherent, or on the contrary, do they dissonate at the typological scale? Moreover, the majority of studies address the inherent set of languages and linguistic structures, leaving the actual typological diversity knowledge out of scope. In this paper, we present and apply the GUI-assisted framework allowing us to easily probe a massive number of languages for all the morphosyntactic features present in the Universal Dependencies data. We show that reflecting the anglo-centric trend in NLP over the past years, most of the regularities revealed in the mBERT model are typical for the western-European languages. Our framework can be integrated with the existing probing toolboxes, model cards, and leaderboards, allowing practitioners to use and share their standard probing methods to interpret multilingual models. Thus we propose a toolkit to systematize the multilingual flaws in multilingual models, providing a reproducible experimental setup for 104 languages and 80 morphosyntactic features. https://github.com/AIRI-Institute/Probing_framework

papers.title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
papers.research_question: Can the internal state of an LLM be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements, both provided to and generated by the LLM?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM internal activations contain information about statement truthfulness and introduces SAPLMA, a classifier that uses these activations to detect false statements with higher accuracy than baselines like few-shot prompting.
papers.conclusion: SAPLMA leverages LLM hidden activations to predict statement truthfulness, offering a way to filter false information and increase trust in LLM-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
SAPLMA achieves accuracy between 60% to 80% on specific topics with OPT-6.7b and 70% to 90% with LLAMA2-7b, outperforming few-shot prompting which maxes at 56% accuracy.
The optimal hidden layer for SAPLMA varies between models, e.g., 20th layer for OPT-6.7b and middle layer for LLAMA2-7b.
Sentence probability assigned by the LLM is not a reliable indicator of truthfulness due to dependencies on sentence length and word frequencies.
SAPLMA can classify both externally provided statements and those generated by the LLM itself.
The method does not require fine-tuning the LLM, using only a trained classifier on frozen activations.
papers.limitation:
The method detects binary true/false, but in practice, detecting uncertainty or confidence levels might be more useful.
Tested only in English; applicability to multilingual settings is not verified.
For longer responses, activation values might need decoupling to isolate the most recent statement.
future_direction: Apply SAPLMA to larger LLMs and conduct human interaction experiments.
Study how activations develop over time as additional words are generated.
Extend to multilingual input and test cross-language applicability.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional performance in various tasks, one of their most prominent drawbacks is generating inaccurate or false information with a confident tone. In this paper, we provide evidence that the LLM's internal state can be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements. This includes both statements provided to the LLM, and statements that the LLM itself generates. Our approach is to train a classifier that outputs the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of the LLM as it reads or generates the statement. Experiments demonstrate that given a set of test sentences, of which half are true and half false, our trained classifier achieves an average of 71\% to 83\% accuracy labeling which sentences are true versus false, depending on the LLM base model. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our classifier's performance and approaches based on the probability assigned to the sentence by the LLM. We show that while LLM-assigned sentence probability is related to sentence truthfulness, this probability is also dependent on sentence length and the frequencies of words in the sentence, resulting in our trained classifier providing a more reliable approach to detecting truthfulness, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability of LLM-generated content and its practical applicability in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: How and where do multilingual language models encode syntactic agreement? Are neurons shared across languages and structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper extends causal probing to multilingual language models, finding two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement depending on distance, significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual models but not masked language models, and that behavioral analyses underestimate masked language models' sensitivity to syntax.
papers.conclusion: Causal probing reveals distinct mechanisms for short- and long-range syntactic agreement in multilingual models, with autoregressive models showing more cross-lingual neuron sharing than masked models, and suggests that models encode syntax similarly across languages but with language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct layer-wise effect patterns for syntactic agreement: one for short-range (adjacent subject-verb) and one for long-range (separated by other tokens).
Neurons are shared across syntactic structures but not with semantic baselines, indicating abstract syntactic agreement encoding.
In autoregressive language models (XGLM), there is significant neuron overlap across languages, but in masked language models (mBERT), neurons are rarely shared across languages.
Neuron sparsity differs across structures (more sparse for short-range agreement) but not across languages.
Behavioral analyses likely underestimate how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information because negative interference from other neurons masks strong syntax-sensitive neurons.
papers.limitation:
Limited to stimuli where subjects and verbs are single tokens, restricting the range of words and languages that can be studied.
Probing individual neurons may oversimplify because complex phenomena like syntactic agreement are likely encoded in sets of neurons.
future_direction: Developing methods for multi-token interventions and variable-length sequences.
Probing multiple neurons simultaneously to causally implicate model regions rather than individual components.
Investigating redundantly encoded syntactic information across neurons.
papers.abstract: Structural probing work has found evidence for latent syntactic information in pre-trained language models. However, much of this analysis has focused on monolingual models, and analyses of multilingual models have employed correlational methods that are confounded by the choice of probing tasks. In this study, we causally probe multilingual language models (XGLM and multilingual BERT) as well as monolingual BERT-based models across various languages; we do this by performing counterfactual perturbations on neuron activations and observing the effect on models' subject-verb agreement probabilities. We observe where in the model and to what extent syntactic agreement is encoded in each language. We find significant neuron overlap across languages in autoregressive multilingual language models, but not masked language models. We also find two distinct layer-wise effect patterns and two distinct sets of neurons used for syntactic agreement, depending on whether the subject and verb are separated by other tokens. Finally, we find that behavioral analyses of language models are likely underestimating how sensitive masked language models are to syntactic information.

papers.title: Metaphors in Pre-Trained Language Models: Probing and Generalization Across Datasets and Languages
papers.research_question: Does pre-trained language models encode metaphorical knowledge, and how generalizable is this knowledge across languages and datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-trained language models encode metaphorical knowledge, mostly in their middle layers, and this knowledge is transferable across languages and datasets when annotation is consistent.
papers.conclusion: Metaphorical knowledge exists in PLM representations, mainly in middle layers, and is transferable if annotation is consistent across training and testing data.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs encode metaphorical knowledge in their representations.
Metaphorical knowledge is concentrated in the middle layers of PLMs.
The knowledge is transferable across languages (cross-lingual generalization).
The knowledge is transferable across datasets but with larger gaps when annotations are inconsistent.
RoBERTa and ELECTRA encode metaphorical knowledge better than BERT.
papers.limitation: Due to resource limitations, experiments were conducted only on the base versions of models.
future_direction: Explore more the cross-lingual transfer of metaphors and the impact of cross-cultural similarities.
Apply metaphorical knowledge for text generation.
papers.abstract: Human languages are full of metaphorical expressions. Metaphors help people understand the world by connecting new concepts and domains to more familiar ones. Large pretrained language models (PLMs) are therefore assumed to encode metaphorical knowledge useful for NLP systems. In this paper, we investigate this hypothesis for PLMs, by probing metaphoricity information in their encodings, and by measuring the cross-lingual and crossdataset generalization of this information. We present studies in multiple metaphor detection datasets and in four languages (i.e., English, Spanish, Russian, and Farsi). Our extensive experiments suggest that contextual representations in PLMs do encode metaphorical knowledge, and mostly in their middle layers. The knowledge is transferable between languages and datasets, especially when the annotation is consistent across training and testing sets. Our findings give helpful insights for both cognitive and NLP scientists.

papers.title: Bridging the Language Gaps in Large Language Models with Inference-Time Cross-Lingual Intervention
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the performance gaps between high-performing and low-performing languages in LLMs without incurring prohibitive costs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces INCLINE, an inference-time cross-lingual intervention framework that aligns source language representations to target language representations using learned alignment matrices, improving performance on multilingual tasks without additional LLM training.
papers.conclusion: INCLINE effectively bridges performance gaps across languages by aligning representations during inference, offering significant improvements with minimal cost.
papers.key_findings:
INCLINE improves average accuracy by up to +4.96 on discriminative tasks and enhances generative task performance.
INCLINE is highly efficient, requiring only 500 parallel sentences for training and adding minimal inference overhead.
Intervention on hidden states is more effective than on attention, FFN, or embedding components.
INCLINE increases correct prediction consistency (CPC) between non-English and English, especially for low-resource languages.
Larger LLMs show greater relative performance gains from INCLINE.
papers.limitation:
Alignment matrices are trained for specific source-target language pairs, limiting scalability to multiple languages simultaneously.
Requires access to internal layers and representations, which is not possible for proprietary or API-only models.
future_direction: Developing multilingual alignment matrices that accommodate multiple languages simultaneously.
Making INCLINE a plug-and-play tool for all LLMs, including those with restricted access.

papers.title: Explainability and Interpretability of Multilingual Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.research_question: What are the current explainability and interpretability methods for multilingual large language models, and what are the key challenges and future directions in this domain?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents the first comprehensive survey of explainability and interpretability methods for multilingual large language models, categorizing existing literature and outlining key challenges and future research avenues.
papers.conclusion: The survey synthesizes research on MLLM explainability, identifies key challenges like the focus on high-resource languages, and outlines future directions for advancing multilingual interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Research on low-resource languages remains underrepresented in MLLM explainability studies.
Existing explainability techniques are often applied to multilingual contexts without significant methodological innovations.
There is a need to expand beyond linguistic case studies to areas such as cultural values, regional variations, and language bias.
The exploration of language-agnostic latent spaces is a promising trend for understanding cross-lingual capabilities.
Explanation faithfulness is a critical challenge, especially for token-based attributions in complex multilingual tasks.
future_direction: Developing novel multilingual explainability innovations dedicated to multilingual contexts.
Advancing work on language-specific features and extra-language knowledge such as cultural values and regional variations.
Improving explainability research for low-resource languages by shifting focus to core NLP tasks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (MLLMs) demonstrate state-of-the-art capabilities across diverse cross-lingual and multilingual tasks. Their complex internal mechanisms, however, often lack transparency, posing significant challenges in elucidating their internal processing of multilingualism, cross-lingual transfer dynamics and handling of language-specific features. This paper addresses this critical gap by presenting a survey of current explainability and interpretability methods specifically for MLLMs. To our knowledge, it is the first comprehensive review of its kind. Existing literature is categorised according to the explainability techniques employed, the multilingual tasks addressed, the languages investigated and available resources. The survey further identifies key challenges, distils core findings and outlines promising avenues for future research within this rapidly evolving domain.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: How Programming Concepts and Neurons Are Shared in Code Language Models
papers.research_question: How do code language models represent multiple programming languages and English in their concept space? Specifically, do they use a pivot language, and can we identify language-specific neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates how code language models represent programming languages and English, finding that English and certain PLs (like C#) are central in the concept space, and that language-specific neurons exist but are challenging to identify for highly aligned PLs.
papers.conclusion: Our findings deepen our understanding of LLMs’ inner workings in the context of PLs and provide valuable insights for interpretability in code-related tasks.
papers.key_findings:
English and PL keywords appear in intermediate layers with high probabilities in the second half of the layers.
C# is highly aligned with other PLs in the model's concept space.
Language-specific neurons are concentrated in bottom layers, while PL-exclusive neurons are in top layers.
For highly aligned PLs (like C# and Java), identifying language-specific neurons is challenging.
The model's concept space is closer to English and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in intermediate layers during translation tasks.
papers.limitation:
The super-parallel dataset is limited to seven languages due to source constraints.
Using keywords to interpret latent embeddings may not be precise because some PL keywords lack direct English meanings or map to multiple tokens.
The analysis is limited to Llama-based architectures; exploring other architectures is needed for broader validation.
papers.abstract: Several studies have explored the mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) in coding tasks, but most have focused on programming languages (PLs) in a monolingual setting. In this paper, we investigate the relationship between multiple PLs and English in the concept space of LLMs. We perform a few-shot translation task on 21 PL pairs using two Llama-based models. By decoding the embeddings of intermediate layers during this task, we observe that the concept space is closer to English (including PL keywords) and assigns high probabilities to English tokens in the second half of the intermediate layers. We analyze neuron activations for 11 PLs and English, finding that while language-specific neurons are primarily concentrated in the bottom layers, those exclusive to each PL tend to appear in the top layers. For PLs that are highly aligned with multiple other PLs, identifying language-specific neurons is not feasible. These PLs also tend to have a larger keyword set than other PLs and are closer to the model's concept space regardless of the input/output PL in the translation task. Our findings provide insights into how LLMs internally represent PLs, revealing structural patterns in the model's concept space. Code is available at https://github.com/cisnlp/code-specific-neurons.

papers.title: Concept Space Alignment in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: Is there a linear mapping between corresponding concepts in different languages in multilingual LLMs, and how does a learned linear mapping generalize to new concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs exhibit high-quality linear concept alignment across languages, but prompt-based embeddings break some of the implicit alignment and generalize worse, especially for typologically distant languages and physical concepts.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs exhibit high-quality, linear concept alignment across different languages, but the ability of supervised maps to generalize varied across different models, languages, and ways of obtaining embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models exhibit very high-quality linear alignments between corresponding concepts in different languages.
Prompt-based embeddings align less linearly than vanilla word embeddings, indicating that some implicitly learned alignments are broken by prompting.
Generalization works best for languages with similar typology (Indo-European) and for abstract concepts.
Abstract concepts exhibit better alignment than physical concepts, which is explained by their higher frequency in training data.
The degree of isomorphism to English is similar across languages, but induced maps generalize much better across typologically related languages.
papers.limitation:
Only six test languages are included due to small overlap between multilingual WordNets, which is too small to draw universally applicable conclusions.
The study is limited to nouns; it is unclear how linear alignment generalizes to other parts of speech.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) seem to generalize somewhat across languages. We hypothesize this is a result of implicit vector space alignment. Evaluating such alignment, we see that larger models exhibit very high-quality linear alignments between corresponding concepts in different languages. Our experiments show that multilingual LLMs suffer from two familiar weaknesses: generalization works best for languages with similar typology, and for abstract concepts. For some models, e.g., the Llama-2 family of models, prompt-based embeddings align better than word embeddings, but the projections are less linear -- an observation that holds across almost all model families, indicating that some of the implicitly learned alignments are broken somewhat by prompt-based methods.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a mechanism in Transformer-based LMs for arithmetic reasoning: information is transferred via attention to the last token and processed by late MLP modules to incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides empirical evidence that LMs process arithmetic queries by conveying information via attention to the last token, where late MLPs generate result-related information, and this mechanism is specific to arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Early MLP layers at operand tokens encode operand information, while attention modules transfer this information to the last token.
Late MLP modules at the last token encode result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
This activation pattern is specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
Fine-tuning on three-operand queries leads to the emergence of the late MLP activation site observed in two-operand settings.
Neuron-level interventions show that the circuits for arithmetic are distinct from those for other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The scope is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division).
Queries are synthetically-generated from natural language descriptions rather than real-life math word problems.
Attention modules are considered as a whole without analyzing individual attention heads.
future_direction: Studying a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expanding analysis to math-based queries in real-life settings.
Identifying specific attention heads responsible for information transfer.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual: Tracing Internal Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How do bilingual language models develop internal representations, specifically when, where, and how does bilingual alignment emerge during pre-training?
papers.core_contribution: Bilingual language models first learn languages separately and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in mid-layers, with larger models showing stronger alignment; bilingual representations are critical for performance, as shown by an intervention method that injects bilingual features from a fully trained model into a mid-training model.
papers.conclusion: Bilingual language models initially learn languages independently and later develop bilingual alignments, especially in mid-layers of larger models, and sparse autoencoders can be used for both analysis and intervention.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs initially learn languages independently and gradually develop bilingual alignment over training.
Bilingual alignments are more prominently captured in the mid-layers of the model.
Larger models exhibit stronger bilingual alignment than smaller ones.
Bilingual representations from a fully trained model enhance the performance of a mid-training model when injected.
The model's internal representations evolve from language-specific to bilingual semantic alignment as training progresses.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on English and Japanese, so findings may not generalize to all language pairs.
The interpretability of sparse autoencoders is limited and reconstruction accuracy is not perfect, so analysis is based on an approximation.
future_direction: Investigate a wider range of language pairs to validate and extend the observations.
Combine sparse autoencoders with other analytical methods for a more robust understanding.
papers.abstract: This study explores how bilingual language models develop complex internal representations. We employ sparse autoencoders to analyze internal representations of bilingual language models with a focus on the effects of training steps, layers, and model sizes. Our analysis shows that language models first learn languages separately, and then gradually form bilingual alignments, particularly in the mid layers. We also found that this bilingual tendency is stronger in larger models. Building on these findings, we demonstrate the critical role of bilingual representations in model performance by employing a novel method that integrates decomposed representations from a fully trained model into a mid-training model. Our results provide insights into how language models acquire bilingual capabilities.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.1, Knowledge Storage and Extraction
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize knowledge during training, and extract it later to answer questions or perform logical reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling) in pretraining data is crucial for reliable knowledge extraction via instruction fine-tuning, and introduces linear probing techniques to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes with practical recommendations for LLM pretraining: data rewriting (augmentation) is important, and including instruction-like data in pretraining is beneficial.
papers.key_findings:
Mixed training (pretraining on both biographies and QA data) enables knowledge extraction, but the model learns in an abnormal way (first from QA then correlates with BIO).
Without knowledge augmentation in pretraining, instruction fine-tuning fails to extract knowledge (0% accuracy).
Knowledge augmentation (e.g., paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) during pretraining enables knowledge extraction after fine-tuning.
Linear probing shows that knowledge augmentation causes knowledge to be linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names, whereas without augmentation it is distributed across tokens.
Including celebrity data (with augmentation) in pretraining improves knowledge extraction for minority data (without augmentation).
future_direction: Studying logical reasoning and knowledge manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can store a vast amount of world knowledge, often extractable via question-answering (e.g., "What is Abraham Lincoln's birthday?"). However, do they answer such questions based on exposure to similar questions during training (i.e., cheating), or by genuinely learning to extract knowledge from sources like Wikipedia? In this paper, we investigate this issue using a controlled biography dataset. We find a strong correlation between the model's ability to extract knowledge and various diversity measures of the training data. $\textbf{Essentially}$, for knowledge to be reliably extracted, it must be sufficiently augmented (e.g., through paraphrasing, sentence shuffling, translations) $\textit{during pretraining}$. Without such augmentation, knowledge may be memorized but not extractable, leading to 0% accuracy, regardless of subsequent instruction fine-tuning. To understand why this occurs, we employ (nearly) linear probing to demonstrate a strong connection between the observed correlation and how the model internally encodes knowledge -- whether it is linearly encoded in the hidden embeddings of entity names or distributed across other token embeddings in the training text. This paper provides $\textbf{several key recommendations for LLM pretraining in the industry}$: (1) rewrite the pretraining data -- using small, auxiliary models -- to provide knowledge augmentation, and (2) incorporate more instruction-finetuning data into the pretraining stage before it becomes too late.

papers.title: On Representational Dissociation of Language and Arithmetic in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What about the language-thought dissociation in large language models? Specifically, are language and arithmetic inputs encoded in separate regions in LLMs' internal representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that language and arithmetic inputs are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space, and that math word problems form a separate cluster, suggesting fine-grained modularity beyond a coarse language-arithmetic dissociation.
papers.conclusion: This study explores the representational dissociation between language and arithmetic stimuli in LLMs, setting a direction to bridge neuroscientific perspectives with LLM internal analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Language and arithmetic equations are encoded in completely separated regions across all layers of LLMs.
The separation is not due to token differences, as spelled-out equations are also separated from language inputs.
Math word problems (GSM8K) form a separate cluster from both language and arithmetic regions.
The arithmetic region activated with primitive stimuli is not used in more complex arithmetic-involved tasks.
There are numerous arithmetic regions for different task formats, indicating fine-grained modularity.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to geometrical properties of the representation space; causal analysis is needed to align with actual abilities.
The generality of findings could be enhanced with other methodologies, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
The topic should be addressed through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
future_direction: Incorporate alternative approaches to identify language and arithmetic regions, such as gradient descent, magnitude of neuron activations, or activation probability.
Conduct causal analysis to test whether the observed geometrical dissociation aligns with actual abilities.
Contextualize the results with existing LM-brain alignment studies.
Address the learnability of specific abilities through different experimental designs, e.g., ablating language learning scenarios.
papers.abstract: The association between language and (non-linguistic) thinking ability in humans has long been debated, and recently, neuroscientific evidence of brain activity patterns has been considered. Such a scientific context naturally raises an interdisciplinary question -- what about such a language-thought dissociation in large language models (LLMs)? In this paper, as an initial foray, we explore this question by focusing on simple arithmetic skills (e.g., $1+2=$ ?) as a thinking ability and analyzing the geometry of their encoding in LLMs' representation space. Our experiments with linear classifiers and cluster separability tests demonstrate that simple arithmetic equations and general language input are encoded in completely separated regions in LLMs' internal representation space across all the layers, which is also supported with more controlled stimuli (e.g., spelled-out equations). These tentatively suggest that arithmetic reasoning is mapped into a distinct region from general language input, which is in line with the neuroscientific observations of human brain activations, while we also point out their somewhat cognitively implausible geometric properties.

papers.title: Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Addition
papers.research_question: How do large language models compute addition? The paper reverse engineers the mechanism by which LLMs perform addition.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs represent numbers as generalized helices and compute addition by manipulating these helices using the Clock algorithm.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent numbers as helices and use the interpretable Clock algorithm to compute addition, providing insight into their mathematical capabilities and potential errors.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs represent numbers as a generalized helix with both periodic and linear components.
The helical representation is causally implicated in addition and other arithmetic tasks like subtraction and multiplication.
LLMs use the Clock algorithm to compute addition by rotating the helices representing the addends.
Specific model components (MLPs, attention heads, neurons) implement steps of the Clock algorithm, with MLPs playing a dominant role.
The Clock algorithm is used across multiple mid-sized LLMs (GPT-J, Pythia-6.9B, Llama3.1-8B).
papers.limitation:
The Clock algorithm might be one method in an ensemble of algorithms used by LLMs for addition.
Different tokenization schemes in other models may require modified algorithms, limiting generalizability.
